title: Copies, references and pointers: which object does a statement reach?
goal: Follow names and pointers to their objects, redirect a pointer, and explain when access is valid.

prerequisites.text: Copying and assignment, scope and lifetime, bool, and simple if from Module 1.
The previous lesson’s expression distinctions and tracing one update at a time.

sections.title: One shared object and an independent copy
paragraphs: Two people read the same counter, while a third writes its old value on paper. When the counter changes, the paper does not update itself. A copy and a reference can express that difference in a program.

value starts at 10. copy records the number, alias refers to the same object, and pointer stores a way to reach it. Predict the three numbers after two changes. In the diagram, A is a symbolic object label, not a real memory address.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and follow the steps
paragraphs: After int value{10};, int copy = value; creates an independent int. int& alias = value; creates a reference to the original object: alias is another way to refer to value, not a snapshot. alias = 12; changes value. Contrast this with lesson 5 copying.

In a declaration, & beside a type introduces a reference. In int* pointer = &value;, * beside the type declares a pointer and &value on the right obtains an address. Symbols have different roles in declarations and expressions; read the complete construct.
If you remove only *pointer = 15, what are the three numbers? They become 12, 10, 12: one change to the shared object is gone, but the copy is still independent.

sections.title: Changing an object or changing the target
paragraphs: pointer holds a pointer value, while *pointer refers to the target object. *pointer = 15; changes value. pointer = &second; changes the pointer itself so access now leads to second. These are different operations and different state-journal events.

A diagram may name objects A and B and draw pointer → A. These are symbolic labels rather than numeric addresses. Actual addresses depend on the run, target, and environment and must not become expected stdout or stable learning-object identifiers.

sections.title: Why a reference cannot be redirected
paragraphs: After int& alias = first;, alias = second; copies second’s current value into first rather than switching the reference. selected = &second; really does reseat a pointer. Observe both original objects when testing or the distinction can remain invisible.

A reference is useful when access consistently names a known live object. A pointer can represent absence or selection, but does not by itself mean ownership. Neither references nor pointers here create or delete their targets.

sections.title: An absent object and an object whose lifetime ended
paragraphs: int* selected{nullptr}; explicitly means no selected object. Check selected != nullptr before reading *selected. The familiar if/else chooses a safe branch: absent when null, or the value when present. This checks absence rather than proving every aspect of pointer validity.

A non-null pointer can dangle after its target leaves an inner block. Checking nullptr does not extend lifetime. Every dereference here targets a live object; null and dangling pointers are never dereferenced, even as a bad experiment. Record that data outlive all access paths in your project.

sections.title: Reading without permission to write through this path
paragraphs: const int* observer = &value; permits reading *observer but not changing value through this pointer. The original value can remain an ordinary int: value = 14; is valid and the observer sees 14. Likewise const int& view prohibits mutation through view. Read-only access does not imply that the source object can never change.

Do not remove const through a guessed cast to silence a diagnostic. The negative example deliberately requires a build rejection when writing through const int*. A constant pointer itself, int* const, can be studied later; the introductory contract focuses on const before int.

sections.title: Checking relationships rather than incidental addresses
paragraphs: The independent task begins with two objects: stock and snapshot. The reference selectedStock and pointer stockPointer should both lead to stock. Before each change, label the object it affects; the model has no separate object containing a “reference value”.

Repeat the operations from initial values 3 and 20, safely within range. Explain the null example separately without forcing a crash. Preserve both a legend-labeled diagram and stdout: a picture alone does not prove execution, and stdout alone does not explain object relationships.

sections.title: Intentional: writing through const int*
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
This access path is read-only.

sections.title: Intentional: a reference without an object
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
An ordinary local reference needs initialization.

deep.title: Does a pointer have to own its target?
deep.text: No. The objects in this lesson are created by ordinary local declarations. A pointer provides access; it neither extends their lifetime nor has a reason to delete them. Ownership is a separate later topic. For now, check that the target exists at every access.

sections.title: Now solve a different problem
paragraphs: Create a snapshot, reference, and pointer. Sell 3 through the reference and add 2 through the pointer. The snapshot must preserve its initial value. Add a second stock object, otherStock{20}. Redirect only stockPointer to it and add 1 through *stockPointer. Explain why selectedStock still refers to the first stock; report both stocks and the snapshot.
Open Practice. Its starter and your current source are separate from the worked examples. Write a prediction before running, then explain the result in your own words.

selfcheck.prompt: After int first{5}; int second{9}; int& alias = first;, the program executes alias = second; and second = 20;. What are first and alias?
feedback: Yes. The value 9 was assigned to first, and alias remained bound to first.
alias = second assigns a number to first; it does not redirect the reference.
Changing second later does not change first: the assignment copied the value 9 only.

selfcheck.feedback: Indirection refers to the target object.

options: No, it copies the value into first
selfcheck.feedback: An ordinary reference is not reseated.

selfcheck.prompt: Does p!=nullptr prove the target is alive?
options: No, lifetime needs a separate contract
selfcheck.feedback: A dangling pointer can remain non-null.

selfcheck.prompt: Can const int* observe a change to an ordinary source int?
options: Yes, const restricts writes through this path
No, the source is frozen forever

practice.title: One stock object, several access paths
practice.task: Create a snapshot, reference, and pointer. Sell 3 through the reference and add 2 through the pointer. The snapshot must preserve its initial value. Add a second stock object, otherStock{20}. Redirect only stockPointer to it and add 1 through *stockPointer. Explain why selectedStock still refers to the first stock; report both stocks and the snapshot.
criteria: The copy is not presented as an alias.
Provide a legend, values, and actual stdout.
No new/delete, pointer arithmetic, or unsafe reads.
Explain in words which object or intermediate value changes. Matching stdout does not replace that explanation.
practice.hint: Add a second stock object, otherStock{20}. Redirect only stockPointer to it and add 1 through *stockPointer. Explain why selectedStock still refers to the first stock; report both stocks and the snapshot.

terms.definition: In our declarations, an alias of an existing object; it needs initialization and cannot be reseated.
A separate object holding a pointer value, such as the address of a suitable live T or nullptr.
In &value, produces a pointer to the value object.
In *pointer, refers to the pointed-to object; access needs a valid pointer and valid lifetime.
A null pointer value; it must not be dereferenced.
A pointer whose former object has ended its lifetime; being non-null does not prove safe access.
